title: The 80% Tax: Why Your AI Projects Spend Most of Their Time Not Doing AI
summary: AI data preparation can take up to 80% of a project timeline. Learn how a continuous, governed AI data pipeline moves AI into production faster.
body_markdown:
### Summary


Enterprises spend up to 80% of an AI project’s timeline getting data ready, and that cost comes back for every new use case, model upgrade, and data source. The fix belongs in the data layer: run the whole pipeline as one continuous, governed service on the storage the data already lives on.


The request arrives as a ticket: “We need the contracts archive available to the new RAG service by end of quarter. About 40 million PDFs. Also, the storage is slow.”


The storage is probably fine. What’s slow is everything between the storage and the model, and the infrastructure team is about to spend the next several weeks proving it.


At Everpure, we[put a number on this](https://blog.everpuredata.com/products/driving-the-future-of-ai-data-readiness-pure-storage-data-stream/) : Enterprises allocate up to 80% of their AI project timelines to data ingestion, cleansing, curation, semantic tagging, and format conversion. It’s a tax, and it gets paid every time there’s a new use case, model upgrade, or additional data source someone wants to add.


## **Where the 80% goes**


A typical enterprise AI data pipeline has[seven stages](https://blog.everpuredata.com/products/everpure-data-stream-ai-ready-data/) : ingest, curate, transform, vectorize, index, retrieve, and generate. In most shops, each stage runs on a different vendor product or open source project, chosen by whoever built that stage, integrated with the next by someone who has probably since moved teams.


The honest number we hear from customers is that it takes two to four months of pipeline work before AI can read a single document. That’s the calendar for one corpus and one use case. Now multiply that by the second use case, the model that gets swapped in next quarter, and the new SaaS export the business wants included, and the tax compounds.


Earlier this year, we commissioned[IDC to survey more than 1,300 IT leaders](https://www.everpuredata.com/docs.html?item=/type/pdf/subtype/doc/path/content/dam/pdf/en/white-papers/wp-why-ai-projects-fail.pdf) , and the results put the other half of the cost in view: One in three respondents said their data scientists spend more than half of their time waiting on IT instead of building models.


## **Why hand-built pipelines break, and who gets the ticket**


Seven stages from seven sources means six handoffs, and every handoff is a place where something can break. A chunking library could change its defaults. An embedding model might get deprecated. The vector index may fill up and nobody scoped a second one. Each fix may be small, but the cumulative effect is a pipeline nobody fully owns.


Governance can break in a similar way. Access controls that existed on the source files don’t automatically follow the chunks into the index, so sensitive content may end up retrievable by people who couldn’t open the original. Nobody planned that, but it’s what can happen when seven tools each assume someone else handles permissions.


And when latency climbs, the ticket lands on infrastructure, because storage is the layer everyone can see. The actual cause is usually a pipeline that copies data three times and stalls the GPUs waiting for the next batch. That’s an architecture problem wearing a storage costume.


You can usually tell within an hour. Put GPU utilization next to storage read throughput. If the GPUs are sitting low while storage is nowhere near its ceiling, the GPUs are waiting on the pipeline, and no amount of faster storage will change that.


A pipeline nobody fully owns is the most expensive thing in the data center after the GPUs it keeps waiting.


## **What changes when the pipeline is one product**


[Everpure Data Stream](https://www.pure.ai/data-stream.html) ™ collapses the seven stages into one automated, continuous, governed product, built on the NVIDIA AI Data Platform reference design and running on infrastructure you own. It ingests from your existing NFS and S3 stores; curates out duplicates, boilerplate, and corrupted files; classifies for sensitivity and applies access controls at the source; embeds, indexes, and retrieves through semantic and hybrid search; and exposes results through industry-standard APIs.


Three things about that matter to the infrastructure team specifically:


- **It runs in place.** No new silo, no content leaving your environment. Everpure Data Stream reads from the NFS and S3 stores you already run, and everything it produces stays inside the security model you already trust.
- **It’s continuous.** The pipeline runs as an ongoing service rather than a one-time project. The two-to-four months of setup goes away, and the ML team’s job shifts from building and maintaining the pipeline to optimizing it and shipping use cases.
- **It’s delivered as a complete integrated stack or as software on the infrastructure you have.** It runs on a fraction of the GPU footprint of other AI Data Platform implementations. Fewer GPUs to procure and place is a line item you’ll recognize.


## **The storage layer still matters**


Storage doesn’t leave the equation here. It becomes the foundation the pipeline is judged against.


[AI pipelines](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/bytes-ai-data-lifecycle/) are throughput and concurrency workloads. Billions of small files, parallel readers, embedding jobs, and inference queries hit the same data at once. A GPU waiting on a file is the most expensive idle hardware in the building, and when the pipeline is one product, the storage performance is what determines whether it waits.[FlashBlade](https://www.everpuredata.com/products/unstructured-data-storage.html) ® is the foundation Everpure Data Stream is built on for exactly that reason, with the headroom to grow from gigabytes to exabytes, and capacity and performance that scale independently so you can add one without buying the other.


That independence is the part infrastructure teams tend to appreciate most. When the ML team’s corpus doubles, you add capacity. When their query volume triples, you add performance. Neither requires a re-architecture, and neither requires a copy.


## **What you own vs. what the platform handles**


After Everpure Data Stream is running, the division of labor gets clearer than it’s ever been on a DIY pipeline.


**Yours:** FlashBlade capacity and placement, network to the GPUs, the access policies at the source, and who gets to call the APIs


**The platform’s:** Ingest scheduling, curation, chunking, classification enforcement, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and keeping all of it current as files change


The ticket from the beginning of this post gets a different answer. The contracts archive goes into the pipeline where it sits. Access controls come with it. The RAG service calls an API. And “the storage is slow” turns out to have been about something else all along.
